prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The monocular depth map captures the continuous receding plane of the dining table from 0.3 m at the bottom edge to 1.2 m at the far edge in frames 1, 2, and 5, placing the nearer salad bowl, phone, and candle within the camera wearer's arm's reach (< 0.8 m) while the far chair back (~1.3 m), left hutch (~1.5–2.5 m), and right wall (~2.5–3.5 m) sit further back. Across frames 1 to 5, the depth gradients reflect the camera wearer's rapid rightward and upward head turn in frame 3 into the adjacent living room in frame 4—where the archway (~2.5–3 m) frames a deeper room with a sofa on the lower right (~2.5 m) and back wall (~6–7 m)—before turning back toward the table in frame 5. The map makes the smooth 3D distance ordering of the tabletop items, the left cabinet's recess, and the archway's separation from the deep living room much clearer than in the cluttered RGB image alone. However, the depth map is unreliable in the distant kitchen doorway (~4–6 m) where the standing person and counter details are lost in uniform black, and in frame 3 where severe motion blur reduces the entire scene to an indistinct, featureless gradient.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map identifies tabletop and room objects in frames 1, 2, and 5, locating two salad bowls (~0.4 m and ~0.8 m, separated by ~0.3 m) and a candle jar (labeled 'cup', ~0.7 m to their right) on the dining table within or just at the edge of the camera wearer's reach, alongside a chair at the far table edge (~1.3 m) and potted plants on the left hutch (~1.8 m) and right floor (~2.8 m). As the camera turns right in frame 4 and back in frame 5, it tracks the spatial shift by detecting a distant TV (~3.5 m) and chair (~3 m, partly cropped at the bottom) in the living room in frame 4, and shows the nearer bowl partially dropping out of the lower frame boundary in frame 5 due to the slightly higher camera tilt. Segmentation highlights exact object boundaries for small or dimly lit background items—such as the distant TV in frame 4 and potted plants against dark furniture—that blend into the surroundings in the RGB frames. However, it is unreliable across the sequence: it completely fails during the motion blur of frame 3, misses the distant person in the kitchen (~5 m) who is facing away through the doorway in frames 1, 2, and 5, and hallucinates 'tv' and 'person' masks on the right wall painting and dark cabinet (~2.5–3 m) in frame 5.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is almost entirely blank across the five frames, showing no valid skeletons for the distant person standing ~4.5–5.5 m away in the kitchen doorway (who faces away toward the sink, partly occluded by the doorframe and out of reach of the dining area) or for the camera wearer's hand holding the phone at the bottom-left (~0.3 m) in frames 1 and 2. Instead, it only outputs isolated, inverted yellow body-and-face keypoint clusters near the bottom edge of frame 2 (roughly corresponding to the nearer salad bowl at ~0.4 m) and the bottom-right corner of frame 5 (on the tabletop clutter at ~0.6 m). While a reliable pose map would clarify body orientation and hand reach, here it offers no spatial information that is difficult to see in the RGB strip. It is highly unreliable in this scene because the actual person in the kitchen is too small, distant, and backlit to be detected, while curved shadows and object textures on the close-up dining table trigger false-positive upside-down upper-body skeletons.
